The Practical Dilemma and Two Avenues of Solution

WHEN WE NEED TO DECIDE WHOM TO TAKE into brief dynamic psychotherapy, we do well to start with the advice of Davanloo and Malan. Their first principle is to exclude patients with obvious danger signs. The second is to try the therapy we are going to use, to see if the patient can work with its potential (Davanloo, 1978), (1980); (Malan, 1979). The idea of "trial therapy" then is simple and straightforward.

If we believe there is only one way to interact with a patient in treatment, "trial therapy" is not mysterious. When we anticipate powerful alternatives from the different schools of psychiatry, however, life becomes complicated: in this instance, contemplating the many possible ways of conducting the "trial therapy" in the selection phase of brief psychotherapy.

IN THE EARLY YEARS OF CHILD psychiatry, preventive mental health was scarcely conceived of. Not until a child presented a florid symptomatology was he of any potential concern to the specialist. Today, on the other hand, a major effort of childhood mental health workers is prevention. This change in emphasis is traceable ultimately to Freud's formulation of the theory of psychoanalysis.

Before Freud, the usual way of thinking about childhood development, insofar as it was thought about at all, was teleological and moralistic. The child was not so much something as he was in a state of becoming something—namely, an adult. Morally and intellectually, the child was unformed, "primitive," and the primary goal of child-rearing was to civilize him. Under these conditions, there was little reason to study the child's way of thinking or even developmental changes in behavior, for these were not phenomena that had value in their own right. They were merely stages in the passage to adulthood.

Such an attitude could not long survive Freud's discovery of the crucial formative function of the first six years of life. The situation was now reversed. Previously, child behavior had always been measured against adult behavior. Now, in the wake of Freud, adult behavior was being referred back to its childhood roots. The key to adult personality lay in the logic of childhood.

This reversal gave rise, in turn, to a second critical development: the scientific study of child behavior outside the clinical context. Instead of simply following received truths on the subject of how children think and act, psychiatrists began, in earnest, to observe child behavior.

JOHN KLAUBER, THEN PRESIDENT OF THE BRITISH PSYCHOANALYTICAL Association, died at 64 in August, 1981, and the world psychoanalytic community lost a seminal mind. Author of Difficulties in the Analytic Encounter (Klauber, 1981), Klauber was trained as a historian, an intelligence officer in the British Army and, later, in both Jungian and Freudian psychoanalysis. Gazing from several theoretical perspectives, "organizing and articulating his self-consciousness in his own erudite way" (Feiner, 1981), he was an elegant scholar with a command of the written language rare among his professional peers. Using the lexicon of Freud, he shares in the book under examination here, the details of his participation in the analytic encounter, and opens to scrutiny analysts' actual work (Witenberg, 1981). His lucid prose is infiltrated with object relations psychology, general systems theory, interpersonalist constructs and sometimes a dash of existentialism and religion. Far too sophisticated and authentically polymathic to attack or to preach, Klauber was content simply to inform, setting forth case material to illustrate and illuminate point after point. He was the consumate teacher-artist, those inspirers of which there are all too few nowadays.

Difficulties in the Analytic Encounter is a collection of a dozen of his papers, published during the past 15 years, now organized into one unified work, with brief chapter introductions which ensure a smooth flow of ideas. DAVID E. SCHECTER WAS APPOINTED training analyst at the William Alanson White Institute in 1962 and supervising analyst in 1967; he was director of training from 1970 to 1974. And he was more than a psychoanalyst. An accomplished musician (he played with the Westchester Symphony), and outstanding researcher and teacher, he brought to the profession a broad intellectual background and passion, as well as his own unique blend of acceptance and quiet seriousness. His attempts at times to reconcile the irreconcilable and at other times to seek out inherent contradictions made him a stimulating teacher on the one hand and a seemingly remote person as well on the other. He held a special place in the hearts of the editors of this Journal whom he encouraged generously and consistently. To the memory of his searching attitude toward life, this issue is dedicated.

David E. Schecter, M.D. 1926-1980

DAVID E. SCHECTER WAS BORN IN Montreal, Canada, December 1, 1926 and lived there until 1951. He received his B.S. at McGill University in 1946 and his M.D. in 1950. He was appointed to the faculty of the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in 1957, and since 1967 had held the rank of Associate Clinical Professor. He was the author of 16 papers and discussions, and from 1964 to 1971 had collaborated on a research project on early ego development in natural family settings.

David's early major interests were genetics and embryology. During his undergraduate years he also had a serious passion for a career in music. He was an accomplished cellist, had played in several symphony orchestras, and more avidly in string quartets.

The move from Montreal to New York, in 1951, was most challenging. To David, who had been imbued with the advantages of a multicultural background, it meant meeting extraordinary people like Erich Fromm, as well as talented artists and musicians. For in New York everything seemed available. But the year he did come to New York City, Fromm, to his dismay, moved to Mexico. Fortunately Fromm returned for four months each year, and David had supervision with him for about six years, as well as some personal analysis.

In 1957, Fromm arranged a month-long seminar on Zen and psychoanalysis at his home in Cuernavaca. David then had the privilege of getting to know Suzuki. In addition to the Zen program, seven psychoanalysts, including Fromm, shared a month of three times a week, two-hour sessions of case seminars. The Fromms also introduced David to the Chinese exercise T'ai Chi, which required grace, balance and a great deal of concentration.

I AM AWARE THAT THE AMBITIOUS TITLE of my communication, "Women's Discourse and Literature: The Question of Nature and Culture, " embraces an extraordinarily vast field of research and reflection. As I address the issue as to whether the difference in woman's expression is exclusively due to culture and not to nature, I want immediately to say that my simple aim is to advance several considerations and to sharpen the focus of some initial questions. Right away I admit that the vastness of my chosen subject makes me uncomfortable, reminding me of the anecdote of the driver who asked directions from a Vermont farmer and was told: "Well, now, if I wanted to go where you want to go, I wouldn't start from here."1 Speaking for myself, I can start from where I am and from what I've got, with the restless solace that my thinking on my subject continues to change.

Nature vs. art, a dichotomy dominant in Greek and Roman thought as well as in Renaissance culture, has now evolved into nature vs. culture, a challenging antithesis for all contemporary social sciences. We all are familiar with the aporias encountered by investigators who try to arrive at laws or principles which are not culture-bound, and we can readily think of the glib generalizations and naive assumptions of former ages in their facile descriptions of the so-called innate in the human being and the harmony of that innateness with world order. Disillusionment about such preordained order and harmony, Freud told us, imposed three narcissistic wounds on the human race. OTTORANK (1945) WROTE, "It is in the act of willing that the human creature becomes creator, both of himself and of those products of his efforts."

Will is the taken for granted thrust for life which we see in the baby who, just learning to walk, falls, gets up gleefully, falls again and who, unable to manage his way to Mother fast enough in this fashion, drops to his knees and scurries to her side. Rapprochement re-fueling is also an act of will.

From the earliest years of life, the developing individual attempts to master challenges. The sense of mastery is closely related to individuation and autonomy. The child who builds and rebuilds his precariously balanced tower of blocks exhibits will in action, and the joy of mastery is his reward. Mastery says, "I can do it!" Will is the energy and determination that does it. Autonomy says, "I can do it all my myself, " and is an expression of the child's individuation and of his pleasure in his awareness of that process. It is a pleasure that is closely tied to the exercise of will and the achievement of mastery.

We see manifestations of will in incredible places and under incredible circumstances, often in acts of heroism. The will to live can sometimes make the difference between actual life or death. Will can also be perverted. We see it in the bag lady whose fierce independence, which we ascribe to her paranoia, leads to her freezing to death in the cardboard house she built for herself on the streets of New York City.

Anita Tenzer  

ARE PIAGET'S THEORIES CONCERNING COGNITIVE development applicable to psychoanalysis? Can his findings clarify the way we conceptualize psychoanalytic processes? Judging from the plethora of references to Piaget in the psychoanalytic literature, many writers think so.

How is knowledge acquired? How do we construct and reconstruct our understanding of the world and our place in it? These questions are central to Piaget's genetic epistemology. The answers Piaget gives apply equally well to the infant's structuring of his world and the child's elaboration of it and to the scientist's explorations and discoveries. He claims that in each case knowledge is acquired through the same mechanisms. If this is so, then it may be that the process of discovery in psychoanalysis is analogous to the child's discovery of his world as revealed by Piaget's experimental observations. It may well be useful to compare our clinical observations and the theories derived from them with Piaget's so as to see in what ways they converge or diverge.

Concepts used in psychoanalysis are sometimes amorphous, vague, hard to pin down. They may require examples in order to be understood. Perhaps by comparing them with Piaget's concepts—concepts that derive from very simple experiments with children—they can be anchored more securely to observable data.

I have selected the concept of insight for this discussion because it is similar to Piaget's concept of la prise de conscience, "the grasp of consciousness" (Piaget, 1974, 1976). Insight, like the grasp of consciousness, can be conceptualized as an active dual process. On the one hand, it makes what is unconscious conscious. On the other hand, it organizes and integrates what is now in awareness in such a way as to make it useful in other contexts.

SUMMARY

Time-limited dynamic therapy is organized around a "focus"—an affectively charged maladaptive interpersonal pattern that pervades a broad range of the patient's interpersonal relationships, including the therapeutic encounter. Identification and systematic examination of this interpersonal focus as enacted within the therapeutic relationship constitutes the primary work of the treatment. As this vignette illustrates, countertransference reactions can provide invaluable clues for identifying the nature of the therapeutic focus. The therapist's countertransference responses reflect his limited participation in the maladaptive focal pattern; the countertransference appears as a reciprocal response, "evoked" by the patient's transference enactments. In the case presented, the therapist felt intensely scrutinized by the patient, as though he was being tested, and he felt a reciprocal urge to be very careful in what he said and how he acted. These personal reactions prompted his initial hypothesis that the patient expected to be coerced and criticized, and therefore needed to remain vigilantly stand-offish while giving only the appearance of cooperation.

Subsequent to this initial formulation, the focus provided a conceptual framework within which the therapist systematically organized his impressions—including countertransference reactions—along a track that kept the therapeutic work circumscribed. Thus, in the latter part of the vignette case, the therapist's realization that he had devalued the patient's expression of affectionate interest alerted him to the continued operation of the initial focal pattern regarding the patient's chronic expectation that her feelings would be discounted and criticized.

In sum, we suggest that the effectiveness of time-limited dynamic therapy may be enhanced when specific attention is directed to discovering and working with the reciprocal relationship between the therapeutic focus and the therapist's countertransference reactions. Each may serve to clarify the other, thereby helping the

621

therapist to rivet his attention to the limited therapeutic radius required of short-term therapies. Furthermore, attention to countertransference aspects of the brief-therapy situation is essential to establishing and maintaining a productive alliance with those especially "difficult" patients whose predominant relationship patterns would otherwise strain the therapist's skill. By viewing countertransference as a welcome treatment ally, the therapist may devote himself more fully to changing the patient, rather than attempting to also change himself by pursuing an impossible ideal of neutrality.

The Two Major Problems in Initiating a Trial Therapy

SULLIVAN (SULLIVAN, 1956) WINNICOTT (WINNICOTT, 1971), AND DAVANLOO (DAVANLOO, 1978), (1980) offer theories of interaction, which attempt to explain their kinds of engagement in psychotherapy. However, all of these must be partial theories, since they explain only a part of the continuum of interaction. A general theory of brief psychotherapy, to be adequate to our practical needs in selection of patients would have to explain how we are to conduct the trial therapy with different kinds of patients. In this paper we will propose such a new general theory.

Let us suppose that we begin, with the customary, "What brought you to the Clinic?" Usually, the patient will offer some details, perhaps some generalizations to explain these details. And usually, the details and the generalizations are inadequate.

IT IS CLEAR TO ALL OF US WHO are interested and active in analytic training that what is called "Control Analysis" forms the basis on which the main clinical instruction in Analysis is built. We are giving

our candidates by a method invented and developed by us something corresponding with the "clinical propaedeutics" in the medical branches, i.e. practical experience with patients under the direction and instruction of the teacher, though in difference with the "clinical propaedeutics" we must eliminate the presence of the patient. This task of the control analysis—difficult enough in itself—is complicated further by another difficulty. The control analyst, as the responsible agent of his institute, must inform it about the fitness of the candidate, a duty whose fulfillment is particularly important when the analyst, to whom the training analysis is entrusted, has himself doubts in the abilities of the candidate. We must also not forget how frequently the training analyst needs this help from the control analyst, in order to find a solution to a frequently arising conflict regarding the qualifications of the candidate. This conflict lies in the double task which the training analyst usually has to perform. The first is the therapeutic aim which must be fulfilled in almost all didactic cases; the other relates to his responsibility as a teacher. These two aims, that of the therapeutist and that of the teacher, often contradict each other.

The successful therapeutical result of a so-called training analysis is frequently dependent on the fact that the analysand, because of his choice of profession, can carry out a great number of wishes and fantasies aroused by the transference, in a manner so adapted to reality. I mean, for example, the identification with the analyst which finds such a successful outlet here, even when the candidate's qualifications are questionable. Small wonder, therefore, if the objectivity of the analyst who may welcome such a therapeutic solution, will fail in judging his student's ability. In addition, there is the counter-transference which may disturb his capacity of judgement, the particular tolerance for his patient, etc. The objective attitude of the control analyst is invoked to solve this conflict. This in itself partially answers the question: Should the control be taken by the candidate's own analyst, or by another? In the Vienna training institute there is no difference of opinion on this subject, but I know there is a great deal of valid discussion about it in other groups and, if I am not mistaken, the Budapest group upholds Ferenczi's preference for the choice of the training analyst as control analyst, especially for first cases.

The Psychotherapeutic Conspiracy by Robert J. Langs New York, Jason Aronson, 1982

IN HIS USUAL FORTHRIGHT manner, Robert Langs has written The Psychotherapeutic Conspiracy (Jason Aronson, 1982), a serious exploration of the failure of present-day psychotherapies and psychotherapists to fulfill what to him is their primary function—i.e., creating a holding relationship and making unconscious expressions conscious by way of understanding the meanings of the patient-therapist interaction. In his preceding writings, Langs focused microscopically on the components of psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy as a means of revealing and treating emotional disturbances. He elucidated the role of the therapist in listening to patients' communications and deciphering their meanings. He identified unconscious communications in dreams, symptoms, actions, and in the therapeutic dialogue. And most radically, he focused on the role of the therapist across a broad spectrum of activities—listening, maintaining a treatment "frame", intervening—in an effort to conceptualize the impact of the therapist on the curative process and to delineate the ongoing ways in which the patient's participation reflects, in necessarily complex and convoluted ways, his/her perceptions of and reactions to the therapist's activities.

Unlike his past writings, however, this book attempts to describe not simply the optimal conditions in which psychotherapy can proceed, but those "deviant" conditions in which psychotherapy is, in fact, conducted, to the ultimate detriment of the patient. Beyond this, he speculates about the factors, from the point of view of both patient and therapist, that might consciously and unconsciously influence either party to accept non-insightful, though at times relief-giving, treatment, or what he refers to as "lie therapy".

ONE DIFFICULTY TEACHING PSYCHOANALYSIS from an interpersonal point of view stems from the current ubiquitous lack of care, interest and respect for persons in our society. In our bureaucratic era, respect for property, protocol, procedures and policy seem to have priority. People are secondary. Now Sullivan was no respecter of techniques as such. He was noted for his respect for those people, who by reason of handicap such as schizophrenia, were given, in his day, short shrift by social institutions, and people, generally. He did respect those who cared for others with difficulties in living, such as hospital attendants. He also was attuned especially to those who tended to the young, teachers for example. As taught by Sullivan, psychoanalysis is respectful of the personal aspects of a patient's difficulties. And in later years, he referred to his treatment as intensive psychotherapy, as did Fromm-Reichmann, to distinguish his approach from classical psychoanalysis. In current society, to which all psychoanalytic students are heirs, respect for the personal dimension has suffered considerable erosion. And this part of Sullivan, this respectful part, fails unfortunately to interest candidates.

Curiously, students are interested in current literature which does stress the importance of the feelings an analyst experiences in response to his patient, cluing him to something going on in the patient and/or the process. However, they do not seem to relate this to an interpersonal theory, which, of course it is. While this is being discussed as part of classical psychoanalysis, which, shamefully, ignores Sullivan, several interpersonal psychoanalysts have contributed to the area.

SULLIVAN, THE FATHER OF INTERPERSONAL PSYCHIATRY, died in 1949 at the age of 57. He left a most valuable legacy, his creative

Copyright © 1983 W.A.W. Institute

20 W. 74th Street, New York, NY 10023

All rights of reproduction in any form reserved.

Contemporary Psychoanalysis, Vol. 19, No. 1 (1983)

140

conceptions which, in the intervening years, have not been done complete justice. They have lost their impetus for a number of reasons. There have been at least two major developments which have stunted the growth of his ideas, independently of some of their inherent weaknesses, contradictions, and the incompleteness of his contributions. For one, the interpersonal model has become an integral part of modern psychotherapeutic and psychoanalytic thought and practice on conscious and unconscious levels. It no longer stands out as the radical approach it once was, arousing our attention to explore it in depth. Interpersonal processes are now viewed either as peripheral, superficial phenomena, by some, or as primary manifestations, by others. Interpersonal events are either treated as the one and only meaningful source of psychological data, or as necessary evils which only distract from the "real" task. And in a similar vein, an artificial dichotomy is maintained between prevailing constructs of the intrapsychic and the interpersonal. This leads to an unfortunate system in which two semantic categories are created, each one to explain what is supposedly the sum of human behavior, internal in contrast to external processes. The result, unfortunately, is an inadequate awareness on the part of the behavior scientist of the dynamic interplay between two dimensions of one unified system. These two factors have complicated the essential task of teaching Sullivan and interpersonalism as one significant dimension of a viable clinical approach to "difficulties in living" (Sullivan's phrase).

Barriers to the Teaching of Interpersonal Conceptions

There are other factors which further complicate the task of teaching Sullivan and interpersonalism. There is a tendency among students of psychotherapy and psychoanalysis to expect to find specific guidelines as to what to do, now and in the future. It is always easier to teach that system which outlines specific steps to follow, or offers prescriptive attitudes, than to present constructs that are basically open-ended and inherently unstructured. The quest for certainty seems to be universal among human beings and the psychoanalyst is no exception. Much may be said in favor of being able to teach the field in a way that can actually provide a clear-cut outline as to what to do and what to avoid so as to reach specific results with patients.

IT MAY BE OF VALUE TO PLACE Dr. Tenzer's interesting contribution within Piaget's own reflections on psychoanalysis and developmental psychology, in particular concerning the issues of the unconscious

Copyright © 1983 W.A.W. Institute, New York

All rights of reproduction in any form reserved.

348

and the conscious. Remembering that Piaget's theory is above all a theory of cognition, means that he is chiefly interested in the way by which intellectual operations, conscious and unconscious, are built, how they come to exist, develop and are integrated and stabilized in the child's mind. Piaget is also engaged in understanding from where these operations derive. He focuses on these aspects of psychology because his purpose is mainly an epistemological one: the understanding of the construction of knowledge and the comprehension of its ontogenetics with the history of science.

Piaget and Freud both explored the relationships between the ontogenesis and the phylogenesis, that is, the implications on a mental level of a biological principle. From that point of view, both were influenced by Darwin.

Piaget is often considered as chiefly interested in cognition but as early as 1920 (as we shall see later) he provided us with insights into the relationship between cognition and affectivity as well as his views about psychoanalysis. Yet his major intent is not a psychological one but a philosophical one. His ideas are never purely speculative. As he cautions us in Insights and Illusions of Philosophy (Piaget 1965/1971) philosophical reflections should only occur within an experimental framework and speculations should always be examined within a context of facts. Here Piaget agrees with Freud, although their methodology differs. The latter used psychopathology to establish facts about knowledge, whereas the former used normal children for his observations. What Piaget does is to extract developmental facts and relate them with their historical aspects.

I WILL BEGIN WITH A BRIEF ACCOUNT of the history of this paper because I believe that will make it more understandable. During the past few years when I have presented my views on the centrality of the analysis of transference and especially on the participation on the analyst in determining how the transference is expressed I have on occasion been asked what was the relation between my ideas and those of Sullivan and later interpersonalists. The question usually implied that there was a strong similarity. Having been reared as a proper Freudian with a more or less unthinking dismissal of Sullivan and interpersonal writings, I was unable to answer. I told myself that I should study these writings, even if I had to risk losing illusions of originality.

What finally forced me to take the question of the relation between my ideas and interpersonal writings seriously was the invitation to present a paper to you. Indeed the invitation referred to a compatibility between my ideas on transference and your views. So I began to read your writings, especially the journal Contemporary Psychoanalysis, but also books by Chrzanowski (1977), Levenson (1972), Singer (1965), and Wolstein (1959). What follows is the partial result of reflection on this reading, which naturally was in the context of how it related to my ideas on transference.

I became progressively aware of an important distinction between two cleavages in psychoanalytic thought which had been more or less fused in my mind.

MUCH HISTORICAL RESEARCH IS required now for developing a fuller knowledge of the current psychoanalytic situation of the 1980s, as it both derives and differs from that of the 1930s. Almost half a century has already passed and we are, culturally speaking, light years away from a uniform, unqualified, and unquestioning belief in the necessary determinism of biology or the relational conditioning of sociology. Neither "environment" of the psyche is absolute. Such a research effort will, therefore, essentially be philosophical in content and reconstructive in scope. Of special interest are two questions. First, from within the standpoint of the ego-interpersonal perspectives, where do such environmentalist psychoanalysts as Sullivan and Hartmann, among others, find the logical and empirical grounds even to create their personal perspectives, let alone account for the uniquely individual, selfic resources from which they derive their own distinctly innovative directions? That of course, is a perspectival question concerning the overall construction of their special points of view. The second question concerns the clinical interaction. Does their systematic exclusion of the patient's uniquely individual, first-personal processes from the structure of psychoanalytic inquiry, in practical terms, also extend the psychoanalyst's authority unilaterally, and reinforce it for managing the procedures and for selecting the goals of the therapeutic inquiry? In other words: Does this exclusion of their own and their patient's immediate experience of first-personal processes mainly appeal to psychoanalysts who believe that it is they, of themselves, who control the conditions under which their patients appear to change? OUR PURPOSE IN SUPERVISION is to teach students that the practice requires the creative use of oneself as well as a sound knowledge of theoretical and technical principles. Mastery of all these aspects of the process is essential to helping the patient toward change, which is, after all, the goal of treatment. The accumulation of knowledge alone is thus not enough. Nor is it enough for the analyst to understand the patient only in theoretical terms. Rather, the analyst must be able to communicate to the patient himself that he is being understood, or the analysis will become a static exercise in intellectual dynamics instead of a vibrant, meaningful experience. We teach students that such empathy (i.e., an understanding of the patient) can only be achieved if the analyst is able to observe his own responses to what the patient tells him in the session, and to use these observations as a sounding board while he listens. Then, and only then, can the subtleties and nuances of the patient's communications be really understood and utilized to expand his awareness.

Although in his own practice with patients, the senior analyst has comfortably mastered these skills—knowledge of theory, the use of techniques related to the theoretical premise, and the creative use of his own responses—in his role as supervisor, he has a more complex task. Whereas in practice it is up to the analyst to "see" his patient as clearly as possible, in supervision the supervisor must develop a picture of the patient indirectly from what the student tells him; he must develop a picture of the student, and he must be clear about the relationship between the student and his patient.

MUCH OF THE LITERATURE ON SHAME begins with the observation that this affect has been ignored, little appreciated, or misunderstood in psychoanalytic writings. This observation has been frequently enough made, in some intriguing and useful accounts, that a substantial body of work on this important subject has accrued, particularly with regard to the differentiation of shame from guilt. Many psychoanalysts have assumed that guilt is the "weightier" subject, and that shame is merely a phenomenon of the ego's response to social disapproval, representing little significance compared to guilt's internal conflicts, the painful war waged between the agencies id, ego, and superego.

With some other authors (Lewis, 1971); (Lynd, 1958); (Thrane, 1980); (Wurmser, 1981) I shall assume throughout this paper that shame is an affect of equal importance, theoretically and phenomenologically, to guilt. I shall also include within the designation of shame those related phenomena of humiliation, mortification, remorse, apathy, embarassment, and lowered self-esteem. While there is good reason to attempt differentiation of these phenomena from shame and from one another, I believe that, for the purposes of this examination, they are closely enough related emotions to be subsumed under "shame" as a signifying affect. Shame has been relegated to second-order importance in classic psychoanalytic literature, I believe, because it relates directly to a construct which until recent writings has not been easily integrated into the mainstream of Freudian concepts—that of the self. Thus, much of the significant work on shame has emerged from writers working within Sullivanian (and other neo-Freudian) perspectives. As we shall see, the classical construct of the ego ideal, a poorly differentiated element of the system superego, has been previously invoked in discussions of shame. That loving function of the superego has traditionally been less accessible than its punitive function, regularly associated with guilt.

A CARDINAL TENET OF TRADITIONAL PSYCHOANALYSIS is that the major curative factor is interpretation, whether of resistances, transferences, unconscious conflicts, or such. To be sure, there have been significant rumblings over more recent decades ranging from corrective emotional or reparative experiences with the analyst or others (Alexander, 1950) ; (Roland, 1967), to the therapeutic or working alliances (Zetzel, 1956) ; (Greenson, 1967), to the real relationship between analyst and patient (Menaker, 1942) ; (Szaz, 1963) ; (Roland, 1967) ; (Greenson and Wexler, 1969), to transmuting internalizations related to developmental deficits and arrests (Kohut, 1971) and (1977). But even with these, interpretation in psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic therapy is still considered to be of major importance for therapeutic progress to occur.

In Hiroshima last summer, under the auspices of Dr. Mikihachiro Tatara, an analyst trained at the William Alanson White Institute and the Austen Riggs Foundation, I had the unusual opportunity to become part of a working group of up to 30 approximately, psychoanalytically oriented therapists from many cities in the Inland Sea area—ranging from Kyoto and Nagoya more in the East to Kumamoto in Kyushu Island in the West—the group also consisting of Dr. Tatara's graduate clinical psychology students from Hiroshima University.

Introduction

IN THIS PAPER I WOULD LIKE to focus on the experience of reality for the borderline patient, as well as the experience of reality for those who are treating him, and show how these are determined by the vicissitudes of a particular quality of relationship which borderline patients tend to form in therapy, that is, what I call transitional relatedness (defined below). A typical sequence in therapy will be presented to demonstrate the problems and pitfalls presented by this quality of relatedness, as well as my view of the process of resolution and cure, which I call containment (defined below). Current concepts of the borderline will be shown as failing to take this into account. The discussion will focus on issues of reality testing, reification, addictive properties of the relatedness, division of therapeutic and caretaking responsibilities, and then touch briefly on implications for the classical psychoanalytic situation with the neurotic.

TTHE CONCEPT SYMBIOSIS REFERS to the living together, in more or less intimate association, or close union, of two dissimilar organisms, as in parasitism. This living together of the dissimilar is usually for a mutual, beneficial relationship. For humans this perforce necessitates an interpersonal relationship or field. And this field, in general, is described by M. Cohen (1953) as follows:

The interpersonal field … is made up of the interaction of a variety of dynamisms of two or more organisms. Some of these dynamisms are conjunctive (for example, the need for intimacy) and lead to an interaction of a situation, with a resolution or reduction of tension; others, which involve anxiety, are disjunctive and lead to disintegration of the situation; sometimes a dynamism can be nonoperative, since there is no corresponding dynamism brought to the situation by the other person. The patterns of interaction are those established in earlier living; and to the extent that anxiety processes have entered into the formation of these patterns, they will be inappropriate and inadequate. (p. xv.)

Cohen is describing an evident social field. I put this at the beginning of this paper because it informs how I perceive the analytic situation. As such it is a basic assumption from which all my assertions follow. Whatever the merits of our high degree of … education, we have lost the gift for being puzzled. Everything is supposed to be known—if not to ourselves then to some specialist whose business it is to know what we do not know… to be puzzled is embarrassing, a sign of intellectual inferiority. To have the right answer seems all-important. To ask the right question is considered insignificant by comparison (Fromm, 1951, p. 3).

MOST PSYCHOANALYTIC SUPERVISORS VIEW THEIR role in the supervisory process as substantially different from their role in the psychoanalytic process and stress the dangers of blurring the distinctions. Levenson's (1982, p. 13) directive to "stay out of the supervisee's analysis," is generally adhered to in principle, although often not in practice.

Supervisors attempt to facilitate the supervisee's analytic work by elaborating technique, by elucidating transference manifestations, by proposing the direction and thrust of the inquiry, and by suggesting appropriate dynamic formulations about the patient or the process. A major aim is to increase the supervisee's ability to observe and explore significant patterns. When the supervisor becomes aware of resistances and/or countertransferences which rest primarily in the supervisee, the supervisee is usually advised to "take it up in analysis." The prevailing notion is that the supervisee's countertransference may be alluded to but not directly explored.

Fromm-Reichmann (1950), Tauber (1954), Searles (1961), and other authors have discussed and elaborated on the positive value of utilizing the analyst's personal reactions to the patient.

IN THIS PAPER I SHALL REPORT ON various aspects of the dreams of patients with borderline personality disorders. I have observed that among such patients, as well as in certain ambulatory schizophrenics who are relatively well-functioning, there are characteristics that appear regularly in their dreams during the earliest stages of psychoanalytic treatment. Moreover, as treatment progresses, and the patient's symptomatology is resolved and overall functioning is improved, there are consistent changes in the structure of the dream narrative and the level of bizarreness. A study of these changes in manifest content may help us formulate some of the shifts in psychic processes which occur during successful psychoanalytic treatment.

As illustrations, consider the following:

Communication A: I was lying in bed. My left arm was disconnected. It was on the opposite side of the bed. I felt opaque.

Communication B: You were sitting on my right side as I was speaking. You were writing something down in a notebook. Whenever you wrote something down, I thought it was important.

Introduction

THIS PAPER PRESENTS A POINT OF VIEW on the psychoanalytic situation and on psychoanalytic technique through, in part, a selective review of the literature. An important underlying assumption of the paper is that existing theoretical models inevitably influence and reflect practice. This is often true even of models that practitioners claim they do not take seriously or literally. Such models may continue to affect practice adversely as long as their features are not fully appreciated and as long as alternative models are not recognized or integrated. An example of such a lingering model is the one in which the therapist is said to function like a blank screen in the psychoanalytic situation.

The Resilience of the Blank Screen Concept

The psychoanalytic literature is replete with attacks on the blank screen concept, the idea that the analyst is not accurately perceived by the patient as a real person, but that he serves rather as a screen or mirror to whom various attitudes, feelings, and motives can be attributed depending upon the patient's particular neurosis and its transference expression. Critiques of this idea have come from within the ranks of classical Freudian analysts, as well as from Kleinians and Sullivanians. Even if one looks only at the classical literature, in one way or another, the blank screen concept seems to have been pronounced dead and laid to rest many times over the years. I. Waking Reality and Psychic Reality

IT WAS FREUD'S (1901) GREAT ACHIEVEMENT to have elucidated the psychology of dreaming: that "the dream is the dreamer's own psychological activity "1 (author's translation; italics Freud's). That the dreamer's psychological activity is a personal response to the perception of external reality is Freud's first and fundamental conception of dreaming (1900).2 This action-reaction paradigm of the dream was a continuation of the insights gained earlier in the studies of traumatic hysterical phenomena.

In the beginning Freud the clinician turned to investigating psychological reactions to traumatic experiences. Trauma, or more precisely the traumatizing event, occurs in external reality and it can be witnessed. The traumatic reaction to the event is private, communicable, and it can be as varied as the individuals and their life histories. Anna O. reacted with "hysterical phenomena" to traumatizing events in external reality. Anna O. suffered from a number of hysterical symptoms which turned out to be "… 'precipitates' … of emotional experiences [to which] we later gave the name of 'psychical traumas, ' while the particular nature of the symptoms was explained by their relation to the traumatic scenes which were their cause" (Breuer and Freud, 1895d). IN A PREVIOUS PAPER (LIPTON, 1977) (AND ADDENDUM, 1979), I attempted to demonstrate that Freud did not change his technique after his analysis of the Rat Man. I learned later that Racker had come to a similar conclusion (Racker, 1968, p. 35). In attempting to make explicit what I thought was implicit in Freud's technique, I wrote that he established a personal relationship with the patient, using a phrase which Anna Freud had used, albeit with some cautionary reservations (A. Freud, 1954, p. 618). I thought that this relationship could not be prescribed or codified, but I described it as restricted (using that word) by its purpose (Lipton, 1977, p. 269) and said it could not be demarcated with precision. AN ANALYST'S COUNTERTRANSFERENCE IS A CONTINUOUS internal response to the presence of an analysand that necessitates a different kind of attentiveness of the analyst's part from that which he gives the patient. Although many patients create through the transference an environment that is favorable to the analyst's good enough state of mind, we are more mindful these days of those patients who represent their existence through the other's moods and thoughts, and, such a countertransference will compel the analyst to take himself as the object of interest, insight, and quite possibly of "cure".

Like many clinicians these days I entertain the possibility that for differing reasons and in varied ways analysands recreate their infantile life in the transference in such a determined and unconsciously accomplished way that the analyst is compelled to relive elements of this infantile history through his countertransference.

WHEN A PATIENT IS FINALLY ABLE TO THINK about a previously unaccepted part of life, seldom are fully formulated thoughts simply waiting to be discovered, ready for exposition. Instead, what is usually experienced is a kind of confusion—a confusion with newly appreciable possibilities, and perhaps an intriguing confusion, but a confusion or a puzzle nevertheless. Unconscious clarity rarely underlies defense. On the evidence of our observations of them as they emerge in awareness, the perceptions, ideas, and memories we prefer not to have, the observations we prefer not to make, are most often murky and poorly defined, different in kind than they will be when the process of completion has progressed to the level of words. "Unformulated experience" is the label I have chosen to refer to mentation characterized by lack of clarity and differentiation.2

NOT INFREQUENTLY IN RECENT YEARS, one hears psychoanalysts expressing an interest in cognition, perception, and learning, often in particular an interest in the body of work produced by Piaget or others with related interests in the development of cognitive processes. Whence this interest? Classically, psychoanalysis has made unique contributions to the study of the development and characteristics of drive, of affect, of conflict, and of fantasy. It has been in the fields of psychology and education, the one more theoretically and the other in more applied ways, where a central focus has always been on cognition, perception, and learning. And yet the two areas have come together with considerable mutual gain. It is the aim of this brief communication to outline, in schematic form, some of the bases and forms of this coming together. In particular, I shall try to illustrate the distinctive contributions that psychoanalysis can make to an understanding of development in the cognitive sphere, in so doing attempting to clarify aspects of psychoanalytic developmental theory itself.

There is no doubt that psychologists and educators have generated an enormous research literature on thinking, on learning, on memory, and on perception. This research is in part descriptive (answering the question: what are thought and learning like?) and in part developmental (how do they change over time?); it is in part theoretical (addressing issues, for example, of the essential characteristics of learning), and in part applied (addressing issues, for example, of how our understanding can help us in education).

THE STUDY OF RESISTANCE HAS NOT, until recently, fared at all well in psychoanalytic research and discussion. Along with some other, at last equally difficult issues, it does not, somehow, seem to stand up to a careful exposition of its historical development as a major defining term of clinical psychoanalytic inquiry. As though to cover up some secret and unacceptable historical origins, its examination has previously earned the dubious status of deferment to some indefinite date in the future. But now, perhaps because current psychoanalytic research is already moving beyond the adaptive and consensual point of view, and as new metapsychology, is also manifesting a far greater concern with the psychology of the self, that future may, finally, be here.

Compare the limited study of resistance with, for example, the many and extensive studies of transference carried out since the matured statement of the classical id model of psychoanalysis of 1915–1917. Or, as further example, compare it with the many and extensive studies of anxiety carried out since the full envisioning of the modern ego-interpersonal (and object relational) models of the 1930s. For reasons that I shall outline in hypothetical form below, it has, to date, escaped the empirical and systematic treatment that, one might expect, so basic a definition of clinical psychoanalytic inquiry deserves.

ANY ONE DEFINABLE INTERPERSONAL RELATION, in so far as it reflects what goes on at all between persons, derives from the psychic activities involving at least two first persons with one another. In the dynamics of psychic experience, it takes at least two first persons to make one interpersona. The cogent and coherent study of interpersonal relations, then, requires the orderly and unambiguous inclusion of the subject matter of the two books under review. For our clinical psychoanalytic inquiry, whenever it concerns the manifestations of the persona—but, of course, always engaging far more of the psyche than its persona—has to deal with the first, the second, and the third persons, in the singular and the plural, as both subject and object. Language is, clearly, a medium of communication, and communication a medium of psychic experience; so while the analysis of unconscious psychic experience cannot, obviously, be reduced to the study of language, it also cannot, on the other hand, be communicated without some form of symbolic representation, including that of language. In these terms do The First Person, by Prof. R. Chisholm, and You, I, and the Others, by Prof. P. Weiss, suggest some general lines along which we may now consider extending Sullivan's conceptions of modern psychiatry, in order to assure the psychological adequacy of his interpersonal-operationist perspective.

H. Racker in 1968 seems to have agreed with him, least of all Freud, whose many technical papers after that marked continuous progression beyond 1910.

I was surprised and flattered to find myself chosen as the paradigm of contemporary standard analysis and I do indeed appreciate the time and effort Dr. Lipton has put into the usual critiques of the silent, neutral analyst. In general, a single session with one patient may differ considerably from another with him, and from sessions with other patients. Therefore the present sampling is just that. I am not disclaiming it—I am making that point before I join in generalizations. Moreover, I am sure Dr. Lipton committed an important methodological error when he dissociated the case from the specific thesis it was supposed to illustrate. The "standard analyst", as far as I am able to judge, does not use Freud's analytic pact and I was trying (not too hopefully) to persuade him to do so. I therefore match Dr. Lipton as a crusader, albeit not a particularly vigorous one.

My approach is actually from a rather suspect side—that of the therapeutic and working alliances, which are usually criticised by the "standards" as oriented to a two-person relationship that departs more or less from neutrality in the direction of helpfulness. Dr. Lipton rather lifts his eyebrows at the notion that Freud in 1938 was still making fundamental new contributions to analytic technique. The fact is however that the analytic pact, as its name implies, is indeed an alliance between the normal ego of the patient and the normal ego of the analyst. The patient promises to say without reserve everything that comes to his mind (free association), the analyst to offer sympathetic understanding and technical competence. I am sure the latter goes beyond silence, which most people can practice with some effort.

FROM JUNE 8 UNTIL JUNE 10, 1935 a Joint Conference (the First "Four Countries Conference") was held in Vienna for members of the Hungarian, Vienna, and Italian Psychoanalytic Societies, as well as the Czechoslovakian Study Group.1 The business meeting on "Training Analysis and Control Analyses" was designed exclusively for members of the Hungarian and Viennese Societies. The purpose was to compare and contrast the approach adopted in Budapest, following the lead of Sandor Ferenczi, with that of the Viennese. (That same year the London and Vienna Societies exchanges guest lecturers on the views of Melanie Klein. The matter of supervision was again a special subject at the second Four Countries Conference in May 1937 in Budapest.) A paper by the Hungarian Vilma Kovacs on training and control analysis2 had stimulated the professional debate, and Imre Hermann opened the discussion with the views of "some" Hungarian training analysts. Although Helene Deutsch was scheduled to speak she was unable to attend because of ill health; Anna Freud then read Helene Deutsch's paper on the "principles and practices of the Vienna Society."3

By 1935 Helene Deutsch was long established as one of psychoanalysis's greatest teachers. She had become Director of the Vienna Training Institute in 1924 and served in that capacity until she left for Boston, Mass.

I WOULD LIKE TO FOCUS IN THIS ESSAY on the early developmental experiences that lay the groundwork—and indeed may represent the necessary, although not necessarily sufficient conditions for creativity. I have in mind here the contributions of Winnicott who pointed to an apparently universal phenomenon in the infant's or toddler's attachment to a soft or hard object which he uses especially when separation from mother or depressive affect threatens him. Winnicott calls the transitional object the first Not-Me possession which may be a blanket, toy, or teddy etc. To quote Winnicott (1958):

I have introduced the terms 'transitional object' and 'transitional phenomena' for designation of the intermediate area of experience, between the thumb and the teddy bear, between oral erotism and true object relationship, between primary creative activity and projection of what has been introjected …

Songs and tunes while preparing for sleep come within the intermediate areas as transitional phenomena along with the use made of objects that are not part of the infant's body, yet are not fully recognized as belonging to external reality.

To quote further:

There is the third part of the life of a human being, a part that we can't ignore, an intermediate area of experiencing to which inner reality and external life both contribute. It is an area which is not challenged because no claim is made on its behalf except that it shall exist as a resting place for the individual engaged in the perpetual human task of keeping inner and outer reality separate yet interrelated.

IN PREVIOUS WRITING I HAVE PRESENTED DATA regarding the creative thinking of Albert Einstein, a man regarded as the leading physicist of this century (Rothenberg, 1979a), (1979b). Close to Einstein in stature—even, according to some, Einstein's equal—was the Danish physicist, Niels Bohr. Einstein's work helped dispel mysteries about the universe, and Bohr's work helped dispel mysteries about the elemental form of nature, the atom. Through his discoveries of the structure of the atom, the structure of the nucleus, his contributions to quantum theory, and his formulation of the principle of complementarity, and through his broad influence as the Director of the Bohr Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen, he was largely responsible for ushering in the current "age of the atom." Like Einstein, Bohr was a theoretician and given to highly creative scientific thought. In the present paper, I shall provide and discuss data regarding Bohr's creative development of the important and influential principle of complementarity, the principle providing the conceptual foundation for quantum physics. For Bohr himself this principle also was a foundation for all of human knowledge. I shall show that a critical step in the development of this principle involved janusian thinking or the janusian process, a type of creative cognition I have previously described (Rothenberg, 1971), (1976), (1978–9).

WHEN I RECENTLY MENTIONED THE title "Self, Will and Empathy" to a friend as a subject I would be writing about he remarked: "Does anyone combine such formidable subjects into one paper?" My answer was that while they are indeed formidable, they are interconnected and it is to their relationship that I wish to address myself. In fact it was a sudden understanding of the interdependence of self and empathy, a kind of "aha" experience, that alerted me to the importance of exploring the interpersonal, as well as the cultural dimension in each of these concepts.

I was viewing a documentary film about recent archeological finds of the Maya civilization in Tikal in Guatemala. I had been there a few years ago when much less was known about Mayan culture, largely because the fuller deciphering of their hieroglyphics had not yet been accomplished. Now we know much more about the structure of their society, their economy and their religion. It has been clearly documented that in their religious rites they practiced human sacrifice. The altars and artifacts as well as the writings concerning this practice have been preserved. To us, whatever our present barbarisms, this is savagery indeed. We cannot identify with it; in fact, we are repelled by it. Whether it was because of the scientific detachment of the young curators reporting the findings, or the facts themselves and the projection of my imagination into that time and place, I was suddenly struck by the extent to which the ritual of human sacrifice at least from our vantage point seems to connote a complete lack of empathy with the victim. Perhaps this seems fairly obvious; yet it raises questions about the nature of the self, its relationship to empathy and the relationship of both to culture.
